[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced ActiveRecord: Associations, Polymorphism, and Self-Joins"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Ruby on Rails provides a robust Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) layer through ActiveRecord. While basic associations like belongs_to, has_many, and has_one cover most standard application needs, complex domain models often require advanced relational patterns. This tutorial explores polymorphic associations and self-joins to build flexible, scalable database architectures."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Polymorphic Associations"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A polymorphic association allows a model to belong to more than one other model on a single association. For example, imagine you are building a commenting system. Instead of creating a PostComment model and a VideoComment model, you can create a single Comment model that can belong to either a Post or a Video."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"rails g model Comment body:text commentable:references{polymorphic}
rails g model Post title:string
rails g model Video title:string"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Running the migration generates a commentable_type and a commentable_id in the comments table. The commentable_type stores the name of the model class, and the commentable_id stores the primary key of the associated record."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Polymorphic Models"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Next, you must configure the models using the polymorphic: true option on the child model and has_many :as on the parent models."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"class Comment < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :commentable, polymorphic: true
end

class Post < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments, as: :commentable, dependent: :destroy
end

class Video < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :comments, as: :commentable, dependent: :destroy
end"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Self-Joins (Recursive Associations)"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"A self-join occurs when a table is associated with itself. This pattern is commonly used for hierarchical data structures, such as organizational charts (employees managing other employees) or social network friendship graphs."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"rails g model Employee name:string manager:references"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"This generates a migration with a manager_id foreign key pointing back to the employees table. You then configure the Employee model to handle the dual perspectives: subordinates and managers."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"class Employee < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :manager, class_name: 'Employee', optional: true
  has_many :subordinates, class_name: 'Employee', foreign_key: 'manager_id', dependent: :nullify
end"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Querying and Best Practices"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use optional: true on belongs_to when the foreign key can be null (such as top-level managers or unassigned comments)."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always specify foreign_key and class_name explicitly when Rails conventions cannot infer the relationship automatically."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Implement dependent: :destroy or dependent: :nullify carefully to prevent orphaned database records."},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"By mastering polymorphic associations and self-joins, you can drastically reduce schema redundancy and build complex, expressive data models in Ruby on Rails."}]
